extracted.intended_audience: general public; readers researching U.S. proposed video-game legislation and rating policy
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia summary of the Video Game Decency Act (H.R. 6120 / H.R. 1531), a specific proposed U.S. federal bill aiming to regulate video-game rating and labeling practices. The page explains the bill's aims, examples motivating it (the 'Hot Coffee' incident), targeted ratings, and its legislative outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit deceptive acts and practices in the content rating and labeling of video games
rubrics_metrics.description: The stated aim of the proposed legislation was to 'prohibit deceptive acts and practices in the content rating and labeling of video games'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the bill's central objective; the page frames it as targeting deceptive behavior in how games are rated and labeled rather than broader content regulation. (Original quoted aim from the page.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent developers from deliberately withholding content from the ESRB to obtain a less restrictive rating
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill would prevent video game developers from deliberately withholding content from the ESRB with the intention of securing a less restrictive rating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page explains why: 'A less restrictive rating would mean that more people could buy copies because the game would be more accessible.' Example motivating incident: Rockstar Games' Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas 'Hot Coffee' minigame—allegedly hidden content that could have led to a stricter 'Adults Only' rating. Emphasis is on deliberate withholding/intent to deceive rating bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target enforcement at games rated 'Mature 17+'
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary target of the legislation was not all video games but those with a 'Mature 17+' rating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites the ESRB definition for 'Mature 17+': 'content that is generally suitable for ages 17 and up and may contain intense violence, blood and gore, sexual content, strong language, drug use, and nudity.' This indicates the bill focused on potentially controversial material commonly at issue in rating disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorize FTC investigations and punish producers found guilty of deliberately deceiving rating organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Pending an investigation by the Federal Trade Commission, the bill would punish any video game producer found guilty of deliberately deceiving rating organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page states that enforcement would be tied to FTC investigation and that penalties would follow if deception were found. The 'Hot Coffee' incident is presented as the factual background motivating such enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restore parental trust by preventing 'end-run' around rating process
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislative rationale: restore parents’ trust in a system in which game makers had previously done an 'end-run around the process' to deliver violent and pornographic material to children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is policy justification rather than an operable statutory test, but it signals the bill's evaluative standard: labeling and rating practices should be sufficiently transparent and reliable to reassure parents. The page quotes Congressman Upton to express this goal.
